Background
Infectious diseases persist as significant threats to global health,
with the rapid spread of pathogen resistance representing a
severe global public health crisis. Traditional antimicrobial drug
development paradigms exhibit inherent deficiencies, including
prolonged timelines (typically 2–5 years) and low efficiency,
rendering them inadequate for addressing the rapidly evolving
challenges of drug resistance. For instance, antimicrobial resist-
ance (AMR) directly resulted in 1.27 million deaths globally in
2019 [1]; furthermore, the development of antiviral and anti-
fungal agents encounters bottlenecks such as high toxicity and
highly mutable targets [2, 3]. Artificial intelligence (AI) tech-
nologies, leveraging their powerful predictive and design capa-
bilities, offer revolutionary solutions for overcoming drug
resistance challenges. These technologies can accelerate the
prediction of pathogen evolutionary trends, the discovery of
novel targets, and the efficient design and optimization of com-
pounds, potentially compressing drug development timelines
from several years to 3–6 months. This article aims to system-
atically elucidate the applications of AI in antimicrobial drug
development, with particular emphasis on critical processes
including phenotype‐driven target identification and validation,
targeted molecular design, and lead compound optimization.

Applications of AI in Anti‐Infective Drug
Development
2.1
|
Applications of AI in Phenotype‐Driven
Target Identification and Validation
AI is fundamentally transforming the entire drug development
pipeline, ranging from phenotype‐driven target discovery and
validation, through efficient optimization of lead compounds, to
precise design of target molecules, thereby significantly accel-
erating the new drug development process (Figure 1).
The evolution of AI in anti‐infective drug development has dem-
onstrated two critical paradigm shifts: first, the transition from
structure‐dependent to sequence‐driven approaches; second, the
progression from single‐target to multi‐target generalization. Early
structure‐based Virtual screening (VS) technologies (e.g., molecular

docking) have severely limited the exploration of novel targets due
to their substantial dependence on pre‐existing target structures
and ligand information. With the advent of deep learning (DL)
technologies, phenotypic screening strategies have emerged as
mainstream research approaches due to their distinctive advantage
of target‐agnostic discovery [4]. Through the integration of phe-
notypic data with graph neural network (GNN) methodologies,
researchers have established a novel “target‐agnostic” approach to
drug discovery. Notable examples include the work of Wong et al.,
who utilized large‐scale compound phenotypic data (39,312 com-
pounds) to train DL models and employed Monte Carlo tree search
algorithms to identify critical active substructures. This approach
led to the discovery of novel antibiotic classes (e.g., N‐[2‐(2‐
chlorophenoxy)ethyl]aniline), which demonstrated significant effi-
cacy against resistant strains and successfully completed in vivo
validation [5]. Similarly, the MolE framework developed by Olayo‐
Alarcon et al. employs self‐supervised learning techniques to ex-
tract universal molecular representations and subsequently inte-
grates phenotypic data to construct predictive models, thereby
facilitating efficient discovery of antimicrobial compounds [6]. The
principal advantage of these approaches lies in their ability to cir-
cumvent the limitations of known targets and directly elucidate the
intrinsic relationships between chemical structures and biological
activities, rendering them particularly suitable for discovering
compounds with novel mechanisms of action. However, these
approaches exhibit notable limitations, including their substantial
dependence on large volumes of high‐quality phenotypic data.

Meanwhile, DL technologies have fundamentally revolution-
ized the field of target‐oriented drug design, particularly dem-
onstrating substantial advances in target affinity prediction.

drug potency and selectivity. Traditional computational ap-
proaches are constrained by limitations including high com-
putational costs and low throughput. Novel deep learning
models such as PBCNet utilize graph attention mechanisms to
accurately predict relative binding affinities of congeneric lig-
ands, achieving zero‐shot learning accuracy (error approxi-
mately 1 kcal/mol) that approaches experimental error ranges,
with performance matching computationally intensive free en-
ergy perturbation (FEP+) [7] methods after fine‐tuning with

In elucidating resistance mechanisms and discovering novel
targets, machine learning (ML) algorithms can efficiently
identify complex resistance mechanisms and novel key de-
terminants that are difficult to capture by traditional ap-
proaches by integrating multi‐omics data and high‐throughput
phenotypic analyses (such as cryptic resistance genes associated
with β‐lactamase activity in Mycobacterium tuberculosis) [8],

novel pathogen variants (i.e., the “cold start” problem), pre-
diction reliability decreases significantly. In dynamically opti-
mizing therapeutic target selection, AI technologies (such
as ML methods combined with MALDI‐TOF mass spectrome-
try) can predict antibiotic resistance of clinical pathogens in
near‐real‐time (typically within 24 h) and rapidly adjust treat-
ment strategies accordingly, effectively avoiding ineffective
therapy [9]. This highlights the unique potential of AI in rapidly
responding to resistance evolution and achieving individualized
precision medication. Nevertheless, the clinical translation of
such methods remains dependent on the widespread adoption
and cost control of automated, high‐throughput detection
platforms, while their predictive accuracy requires continuous
validation in larger‐scale, more complex real‐world clinical
samples. In elucidating resistance mechanisms and discovering
novel targets, ML algorithms can efficiently identify complex
resistance mechanisms and novel key determinants that are
difficult to capture by traditional approaches by integrating
multi‐omics data and high‐throughput phenotypic analyses
(such as cryptic resistance genes associated with β‐lactamase
activity in Mycobacterium tuberculosis), which fully demon-
strates their powerful hypothesis‐free screening capability and
advantages in handling high‐dimensional data. However, their
performance is inherently constrained by the quality, scale,
representativeness, and annotation accuracy of training data;
for rare mechanisms or novel pathogen variants (i.e., the “cold
start” problem), prediction reliability decreases significantly.

In developing multi‐target synergistic intervention strategies, deep
learning and other AI models can reveal candidate molecules
with multi‐pathway inhibition potential by parsing complex
compound‐target interaction networks (for instance, novel anti-
biotics screened by Wong et al. through explainable AI models)
[5], which not only provide new insights for overcoming single‐
target resistance but also facilitate the elucidation of synergistic
mechanisms. However, designing multi‐target molecules that
simultaneously possess efficient synergistic activity, favorable
pharmacokinetic properties, and low toxicity remains a significant
challenge. The predictive accuracy of deep learning models is
highly dependent on the coverage of high‐quality interaction data,
while their inherent complexity presents interpretability chal-
lenges that, although improved, still have room for enhancement.
Key challenges include: constructing more comprehensive and
reliable biomolecular interaction databases, developing more
advanced explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) methods to guide
rational multi‐target design, and balancing multi‐target activity
with safety risks posed by potential off‐target effects.
AI demonstrates significant potential in drug repurposing by
analyzing chemical features and known target interaction patterns
through DL algorithms, thereby enabling the prediction of
potential new indications. For instance, in COVID‐19 research, AI‐
driven knowledge graphs successfully predicted the therapeutic
efficacy of Remdesivir (a viral RNA polymerase inhibitor) and
Baricitinib (a rheumatoid arthritis treatment that blocks viral entry
by targeting the host AAK1 protein), both of which have been
validated through clinical trials [10]. For the mpox virus, ML
models identified antifungal agents such as Amphotericin B,
which can inhibit infection by disrupting viral membrane lipid raft
structures [11]. In HCMV research, AI further revealed that the
virus promotes glycolysis through AMPK pathway activation, and
pathway inhibitors targeting this mechanism can significantly
reduce viral replication [12]. Although clinical validation remains
necessary, AI nevertheless provides another viable approach for
drug repurposing. Furthermore, AI can integrate electronic health
records with multi‐omics data, revealing that the diabetes medi-
cation metformin may reduce the risk of severe COVID‐19
through metabolic pathway modulation [10].

Applications of AI in Target Molecular
Design
In anti‐infective drug development, target molecular design
represents a fundamental component of drug discovery, en-
compassing two distinct technological approaches: screening

strategies based on existing molecular libraries and structure‐
based de novo design methods. In the field of molecular
screening, two synergistic and complementary technologies
predominate: VS achieves target–ligand interaction prediction
through computational chemistry simulation, significantly en-
hancing lead compound identification efficiency. Conversely,
high‐throughput screening relies on automated platforms to
validate the biological activity of millions of compounds and is
regarded as the definitive gold standard for experimental vali-
dation. These two screening modalities generate substantial
synergistic effects in drug development practice, thereby facili-
tating the efficient enrichment and identification of candidate
molecules from vast compound libraries.
VS exhibits remarkable efficacy in addressing the challenges
posed by billion‐scale compound libraries through AI‐driven
technological innovations: For instance, the BaCNet model
integrates bacterial protein ESM‐2 embeddings with compound
fingerprints, successfully screens candidate molecules targeting
Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and achieves a threefold improve-
ment in experimental success rates through molecular dynam-
ics validation, thereby highlighting AI's breakthrough in multi‐
source information integration and screening efficiency [13].
Deep neural networks further transcend traditional structural
constraints by discovering Halicin, a broad‐spectrum anti-
microbial molecule highly effective against MRSA, from a
library of 107 million molecules, thereby demonstrating AI's
capability to explore nonclassical chemical space [14]. Fur-
thermore, GNNs identify and validate the G1–G5 series of an-
timicrobial agents containing chlorobenzene ring scaffolds
through interpretable strategies, thus demonstrating AI's un-
ique value in structural feature analysis [15].
The dynamic optimization capabilities of AI in anti‐infective
drug experimental design are significantly transforming drug
screening paradigms: The EvoDesign platform achieves a 60%
reduction in experimental cycles by utilizing evolutionary al-
gorithms to generate SARS‐CoV‐2 Spike protein variants and
guide antigenic epitope screening in pseudovirus neutralization
assays [16]; its core advantage lies in precisely substituting high‐
cost trial‐and‐error approaches with computational simulation,
thereby accelerating epitope localization. Simultaneously, ML
models in antimicrobial peptide screening enhance MRSA
detection sensitivity by 30% through dynamic adjustment of
concentration gradients based on predicted MIC distributions,
while incorporating chemical clustering to prioritize syntheti-
cally accessible molecules, fully highlighting AI's unique value
in resource allocation optimization and synthetic feasibility
prediction [17].
AI‐driven de novo drug design is profoundly revolutionizing the
traditional molecular design paradigm that relies on expert‐based
rules: for instance, the AMPredictor framework, which integrates
generative adversarial networks with graph convolutional net-
works, successfully designed 16 bifunctional peptide molecules
(e.g., P076 demonstrated an MIC of 0.21 μM against multidrug‐
resistant Acinetobacter baumannii with superior safety compared
to polymyxin B) [18]; Additionally, variational autoencoders
(VAEs) combined with cell‐free protein synthesis (CFPS) tech-
nology screened 30 effective antimicrobial peptides from 500
candidates within 24 h (including 6 broad‐spectrum molecules
against ESKAPE pathogens that did not induce resistance in the
short term) [19], demonstrating AI's remarkable breakthrough in
rational design and ultra‐rapid validation of multifunctional pep-
tides. However, these “efficient innovations” harbor significant
technical risks and biological limitations. First, functional diversity
presents notable defects: the bifunctional peptides (antibacterial/
antiviral) designed by AMPredictor may exhibit folding stability
defects due to functional domain conflicts (e.g., the α‐helical am-
phiphilicity of P076 may be compromised by dual active sites), and
the safety advantages demonstrated in mouse models remain
questionable in long‐term toxicological assessments. Second,
clinical translation validity remains questionable: the activity of
VAE‐generated peptides rapidly validated through CFPS only
reflects cell‐free environment performance (which overlooks the
degradative effects of mammalian serum proteases), and the so‐
called “non‐resistance‐inducing” conclusion stems from 72‐h
short‐term exposure experiments, thus failing to simulate the
authentic pressure of clinical resistance evolution.
2.3
|
Applications of AI in Lead Compound
Optimization
DL significantly enhances the activity of lead compounds by
optimizing their spatial conformations at target sites. Taking the
TransSAFP model as an example, this model ingeniously inte-
grates pre‐training and transfer learning modules to accurately
analyze the secondary structures of peptide sequences (such as α‐
helices/β‐sheets) and their self‐assembly propensities. Meanwhile,
through N‐terminal modifications (e.g., C12 alkyl chains, BIP
aromatic groups), it further optimizes hydrophobic interactions
and π‐π stacking, thereby achieving integrated conformation‐
function synergistic regulation. Experimental results confirm that
the AI‐designed p45 peptide exhibits a critical assembly concen-
tration (CAC) as low as 6 μg/mL and spontaneously forms nano-
fiber structures. This structure disrupts bacterial membrane
integrity and demonstrates broad‐spectrum antimicrobial activity
against 14 pathogens, including 5 drug‐resistant strains (MIC
3–66 μg/mL), with no observed resistance induction phenomenon
[20]. This technology significantly reduces the traditional “trial‐
and‐error” design cycle by up to 80%, thereby providing an effi-
cient and intelligent optimization strategy for developing small‐
molecule peptide drugs with clear targeting and excellent stability.
A major bottleneck in traditional anti‐infective drug development
is the inadequate prediction or incomplete characterization of
potential absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, and
toxicity (ADMET) properties [21]. AI exhibits remarkable potential
for enabling early and accurate prediction of drug ADMET prop-
erties, thereby significantly enhancing the success rate of subse-
quent drug development. DL, as a core branch of AI, is
revolutionizing ADMET prediction by efficiently and automati-
cally extracting high‐dimensional meaningful features from multi‐
source heterogeneous input data. Various advanced neural net-
work architectures, including Transformer models designed for
efficient sequential data processing, convolutional neural networks
that excel in image and video recognition tasks, and GNNs that
have recently emerged for handling graph‐structured molecular
data, have demonstrated superior performance in accurately
modeling molecular properties based on diverse formats including
SMILES strings and molecular graphs.

Limitations and Future Directions
The application of AI in anti‐infective drug development faces
multiple challenges (Figure 2). Firstly, data quality has a direct
impact on model reliability and performance (e.g., incomplete
or erroneous data); to address this challenge, establishing
standardized experimental protocols to generate high‐quality
data, coupled with the creation of high‐quality pseudo‐samples,
optimization of feature selection techniques, and development
of prediction error quantification tools, is crucial for strength-
ening the data foundation [22]. Secondly, model generalizability
requires urgent improvement, particularly given its limited
applicability when addressing new environments, novel hosts,
or emerging pathogens; by integrating real‐time tracking

for drugs targeting emerging infectious diseases can be signifi-

models results in poor interpretability, with the reliability of
their conclusions still requiring rigorous validation through wet
laboratory experiments; in light of this limitation, actively
applying explainable AI (XAI) technologies and deeply inte-
grating them with pathogen‐host‐drug knowledge graphs rep-
resents an effective strategy for promoting the “white‐box”
transformation of drug development workflows, thereby sig-
nificantly enhancing transparency and improving trustworthi-
ness [23]. Finally, the efficient and seamless integration of key
AI steps into existing anti‐infective drug development work-
flows to achieve optimal synergistic effects requires careful
consideration and planning; this undoubtedly relies heavily on
deep involvement of researchers with professional expertise and
practical experience, as well as robust support from compre-
hensive
infrastructure
and
high‐performance
computing
resources.
Through
systematically
addressing
these
challenges—namely, comprehensively improving data quality,
continuously
enhancing
model

effectively
increasing interpretability, and optimizing the integration of
drug development workflows—AI has the potential to more
efficiently empower all critical aspects of anti‐infective drug
development, thereby significantly improving development
efficiency and success rates, and ultimately driving major
innovations
across
the
entire
anti‐infective
field.
This
advancement will be particularly valuable in responding to
public health emergencies, where AI's capabilities could prove
transformative.
